\begin{bankq}[id=SI11-P1-PHY-S3-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 11 (27 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=numerical, subtopic={Friction}, answer={25.60}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: finger positions when a metre scale slips on two fingers, different friction | steps: normal forces inversely related to distances from centre; static friction limit of the stationary finger equals kinetic friction of the slipping finger; x_R from the ratio of mu_s and mu_k | I: alternating slipping condition between fingers}]
Put a uniform meter scale horizontally on your extended index fingers with the left one at 0.00 cm and the right one at 90.00 cm. When you attempt to move both the fingers slowly towards the center, initially only the left finger slips with respect to the scale and the right finger does not. After some distance, the left finger stops and the right one starts slipping. Then the right finger stops at a distance $x_R$ from the center (50.00 cm) of the scale and the left one starts slipping again. This happens because of the difference in the frictional forces on the two fingers. If the coefficients of static and dynamic friction between the fingers and the scale are 0.40 and 0.32, respectively, the value of $x_R$ (in cm) is \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}.-
\end{bankq}

\opt{A}{$v_0^2-2gh=\dfrac12gR$}
\opt{B}{$v_0^2-2gh=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2gR$}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SI12-P2-PHY-S1-G3-4, source={Score-I - Test 12 (09 Mar 2022)}, questions={3-4}]

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{|p{0.8cm}|p{3.6cm}|p{0.8cm}|p{3.8cm}|p{0.8cm}|p{3.8cm}|}
\hline
 & \centering Column-I & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{Column-II} & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{Column-III}\\
\hline
(I) & \bfigi{66.1}{SI12_p2_phy_s1_para3_4_1.png}\rule{0pt}{35pt} & (i) & $W_2=(2m-M)\dfrac g3$ & (P) & $W_1=(m+M)\dfrac g3$\\
\hline
(II) & \bfigi{77.0}{SI12_p2_phy_s1_para3_4_2.png}\rule{0pt}{45pt} & (ii) & $W_2=(2m-M)\dfrac g2$ & (Q) & $W_1=(m+M)\dfrac g2$\\
\hline
(III) & \bfigi{67.5}{SI12_p2_phy_s1_para3_4_3.png}\rule{0pt}{42pt} & (iii) & $W_2=(m-M)\dfrac g4$ & (R) & $W_1=(m+M)g$\\
\hline
(IV) & \bfigi{52.9}{SI12_p2_phy_s1_para3_4_4.png}\rule{0pt}{33pt} & (iv) & $W_2=(3m-M)\dfrac g4$ & (S) & $W_1=(m+M)\dfrac g4$\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{bankq}[id=SII44-P1-PHY-S2-Q05, source={Score-II - Test 44 (23 Mar 2025)}, paper=1, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={Friction}, answer={Bonus}, answer_src=solved, working={Printed key covers only one subject (chemistry) and this question was not solved; banked as Bonus.}, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: friction of two rotating rollers on a rod, restoring or repelling force | steps: friction on the nearer roller is larger so the net force is proportional to the displacement from the centre; for opposite rotations the force is restoring giving simple harmonic motion with w^2 = 2 mu g/a; reversed rotation gives exponential growth with the same constant; check the four expressions}]
A uniform thin rigid rod of mass m is supported by two rapidly rotating rollers, whose axes are separated by a fixed distance a. The rod is initially placed at rest symmetrically as shown in Fig.1. Assume that the rollers rotate in opposite directions as shown in fig.1. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the rod and the rollers is $\mu$. Now consider the case in which the direction of rotation of the rollers are reversed, as shown in fig.2. (Assume x = x$_0$ and v = 0 at t = 0 for both cases.)

\begin{center}
\bfigi{233.8}{SII44_p1phy_q5_rollers.png}
\end{center}

(A) For case shown in fig.1
$$x(t)=\left(x_0-\dfrac a2\right)\cos\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{2\mu g}a}t\right)+\dfrac a2.$$

(B) For case shown in fig.2
$$\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{$x(t)=\left(x_0-\dfrac a2\right)\left(\dfrac{e^{-2\omega t}+e^{2\omega t}}2\right)+\dfrac a2,\text{ where }\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\mu g}a}.$}$$

(C) For case shown in fig.2
$$x(t)=\left(x_0-\dfrac a2\right)\cos\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{2\mu g}a}t\right)+\dfrac a2.$$

(D) For case shown in fig.2
$$x(t)=\left(x_0-\dfrac a2\right)\left(\dfrac{e^{\omega t}+e^{-\omega t}}2\right)+\dfrac a2,\text{ where }\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\mu g}a}.$$
\end{bankq}
